episode_thesis: Jeffrey Hirsch argues that market calendar patterns (four-year/midterm cycle, best six months Nov-Apr, January barometer, monthly and intraday flows, sector seasonals) persist because people and institutions behave habitually and rebalance on calendar dates, and that algorithms inherit these habits because people program them. He treats seasonality as an average tendency that must be combined with technicals, fundamentals, monetary policy and sentiment and re-checked as patterns decay, and he adds a long-run super-boom thesis (war plus inflation plus a paradigm-shifting technology, now AI). Host Steve Eisman supplies the window-dressing mechanism, is sceptical of Bitcoin and sees a credit-cycle tightening from private credit.

worldview_premises.premise: Seasonal structure persists in the algorithmic era because humans programme the algorithms.

worldview_premises.premise: The midterm year is weak mid-year because campaigning draws attention from markets and leaves them vulnerable to shocks; 11 of the last 16 bear markets bottomed in a midterm year.

worldview_premises.premise: Mutual-fund fiscal year end (40 Act, October 31) and quarter-end flows, year-end performance chasing and holiday money drive the best-six-months pattern.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Hirsch tests only one seasonal rule (best six months) out of sample; the many other patterns (midterm cycle with few observations, January trifecta 29 of 32, Trump pattern from five years) have no multiple-testing adjustment or out-of-sample test.

Hirsch says patterns decay (September reverse barometer, small-cap January effect, monthly turn-of-month pattern) and that seasonal rules are averages, yet presents surviving patterns as reliable; no criterion for retiring a pattern is given.
The 401(k) 'super eight days' pattern is described as a mechanism and also as something Hirsch and his partner argue about every year.
The causal story for the January barometer (20th Amendment, inauguration date) is a narrative, not tested; Hirsch uses it to explain what he calls statistically true.
The Bitcoin seasonal is admitted to have too little data, yet its failure is treated as a signal of 'something wrong' via Gul's rule.
The super-boom thesis reads the 2011 inflation condition loosely (no war inflation, so COVID spending is used instead); the 500% target depends on the choice of low (2009 vs 2011).
The transcript is ambiguous on whether Eisman thinks private credit is a systemic issue; the caption reads 'I don't think private credit has some really serious problems. It's a systemic issue'.
Window-dressing claim was first attributed to Hirsch; it is Eisman's explanation that Hirsch endorsed (ledger correction applied).
Hirsch says the Almanac did not foresee the Iran war and that exogenous events override seasonality; he nonetheless offers war-duration rules (bottom within about a month) derived from past wars.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Calendar position (midterm-year Q2-Q3 low, Q4 to Q2 sweet spot, pre-election December high), October 31 fund fiscal year end and quarter-end flows, January trifecta, MACD momentum as confirmation, monthly payroll inflows, war duration and oil, and signs of private-credit stress. Horizons are days (intraday and monthly flows), months (best six months, sector seasonals) and years (four-year cycle, super boom to about 2030).
reader_inferences: (reader) Hirsch's evidence is mostly historical averages with small samples for rarer cycles (eleven of sixteen bear markets; five Trump years), so the claims about timing within the year are weaker than the long-run best-six-months result.
(reader) The flow mechanisms (fiscal year end, 401(k) inflows) could be tested with fund flow data; the 401(k) effect would be expected to fade as flows are better anticipated.
(reader) Hirsch combines seasonality with confirmation rules (MACD, technical entry), which makes the system a filter on seasonal tendency, not a stand-alone signal.
(reader) Eisman's and Hirsch's views are not in conflict on mechanism; they differ on how serious the private-credit risk is.
